newsitem.title: USA: IRS issues technical ruling on audited bond deals.
newsitem.headline: IRS issues technical ruling on audited bond deals.

text.p: The Internal Revenue Service issued the first in a string of technical advisory rulings on the tax-exempt status of bonds that the agency is reviewing under its audit program.
The Service said in an eight-page ruling that some of the interest on a certificates of participation offering by an unnamed locality is not tax exempt.

IRS officials said recently that they have roughly 270 bond issues under random and targeted audit as of April 1997 and that the Service has reached between six and eight closing agreements totaling millions of dollars since early 1996.
IRS issues two kinds of rulings in connection with examinations of tax-exempt bonds.

"Private letter rulings" go to bond issuers that request feedback on the taxability of bonds before they actually issue them. "Technical advisory memoranda," on the other hand, go to IRS field staff seeking feedback from headquarters on already issued bonds that they are investigating.
Amy Dunbar, director of governmental affairs for the National Association of Bond Lawyers, said the technical ruling "shows that IRS' enforcement effort is maturing."
"We haven't seen many of these before because they weren't bringing enforcements or because the parties were settling prior to the formal issuance of technical advice," Dunbar said.
"It is a statement ... that they are bringing more cases and that the parties are not agreeing to settle quietly. Sort of like a poker game - you want to see the other guy's hand," Dunbar said.
IRS said in the new ruling, "The Service has ruled that a syndicated financing arrangement that resembled a line of credit for state districts did not pay interest excludable from gross income."

"Several districts entered into a financing agreement under which they transferred notes to an investment trust that sold COPs to the public. The trust invested the proceeds ... in a taxable investment fund," IRS said.
"The districts had the right to draw on the funds in the trust, but not all did so. A district's obligation to pay interest on its notes arose only when it actually withdrew funds."

"The Service concluded that the transaction resembled a revolving line of credit more than a transaction in which the only assets held by the trust" were tax exempt "despite efforts of the parties to make the financing appear to be borrowings by state and local governments," IRS said.
